1:
Charles Ellicott opens the chapter by setting out, before any verse is expounded, the question it will raise about the sign given later. He states the first reading as if the Gospel had never been written: the prophet points to some young bride, says she shall bear a son, and the fulfilment of a prediction lying outside human knowledge is the sign, the name Immanuel witnessing not to an incarnate Deity but to a living presence. Who the mother was there are no data for deciding—the likeliest conjecture is the prophet’s own wife, others guessing a woman of the king’s household; and the theory that she bore Hezekiah breaks down, he says, under the test of dates, Hezekiah being already a boy of nine. The second reading takes the evangelist’s citation as settling everything, the prophet in ecstasy seeing the incarnation. Ellicott lists the difficulties frankly. A sign is soon tested by experience, and a prophet stakes his reputation on it; how could a birth several centuries off be a sign to Ahaz? What would butter and honey mean of such a child? Do not the words about the child not yet knowing to refuse the evil point to one growing up in that generation? And should we not expect the prophet to dwell on so great a mystery elsewhere, later prophets to name it, the Jewish schools to keep it—none of which happened? He turns that last point round: it is among the strongest arguments for the historical character of the nativity narratives that they ran contrary to prevailing expectation.

Ellicott then offers a third way. The evangelist elsewhere detaches predictions from settings where they had a distinct historical meaning and gives them a new one; and the explanation is not that facts were invented so prophecies might seem fulfilled, but that, the facts being given, prophecies were shown to have a meaning fulfilled in them which may never have been present to the prophet’s mind. He adds the limits within which prophets worked: they enquired and searched about the time and manner of what they hoped for, their normal state being enquiry rather than assurance, so they looked for their ideal king as near at hand. They were not altogether wrong, since prophecy has its springing and germinant accomplishments.

On the history the others supply what Ellicott passes over. John Calvin insists this is the second war and not the first: in the earlier one Ahaz was beaten and a multitude carried off, and the kings came again because they judged him worn out—which is what makes the deliverance a miracle. Matthew Henry accounts for the silence of the record under the previous reign by supposing many useful sermons were preached and never published, and that under a wicked king the prophet had less opportunity at court and so wrote the more. He notes that the degenerate family is still called the house of David, recalling the promise that transgression would be chastened but the loving-kindness not taken away. John Gill explains the three royal names as fixing the prophecy’s date, not, as the Jewish writers say, crediting the ancestors’ worthiness with the failure of the invasion. Adam Clarke maps the next three chapters, admitting of one part that he attempts no particular explanation, calling it very difficult. Keil and Delitzsch distinguish a phrase: the verb rendered is confederate with means settled down upon, elsewhere a hostile invasion, here one army arriving to support another. Calvin canvasses the same verb and reports three derivations. He uses the panic to draw a contrast: the ungodly in prosperity hardly believe they are under God’s government and are stunned by adversity till they lie as men bereft of their senses, while the godly may be shaken but betake themselves to a safe harbour. John Wesley notes the paradox: no prophecies are more comfortable than those delivered under so impious a king.
3:
Charles Ellicott finds the king halting between two opinions. He is making a show of resistance, but depends neither on the protection of God nor on the courage of his people, but on a plan of his own: to keep paying tribute to Assyria and write to Tiglath-pileser to attack the invaders’ territories, as he later did. He was apparently superintending the defensive works, cutting off the water outside the walls. John Calvin reads the meeting differently—God, remembering his covenant, anticipates this wicked king, not waiting for his prayers but of his own accord promising deliverance; the running about in all directions is itself the evidence of dread in a wretched hypocrite. On the son who goes with him, both agree the name is the message. Calvin holds it was not given at random but by the secret inspiration of the Spirit, the boy carrying an engraven seal both of the approaching captivity and of the return; John Wesley reads it as a sign and pledge, the remnant shall return. Ellicott adds that he was probably then a stripling of sixteen or eighteen, and notes an earlier prophet whose children were given names terribly or hopefully significant. Keil and Delitzsch place the fuller’s field on the western side of the city, by an upper pool of great antiquity; there the cleaners and thickeners of woollen fabrics worked, and travellers have seen the ground round it covered with things spread to bleach or dry.

The charge to keep quiet draws out the philologists. John Gill takes it as keeping oneself not from fighting but from unbelief and dread, and reports the Jewish reading of settling, as wine upon its lees; Keil and Delitzsch judge that sense hardly suits, and divide the two imperatives—the first warns against acting for himself in estrangement from God, the second exhorts to a calm secured by confidence in him, which they gloss from Calvin as restraining himself outwardly and keeping his mind calm within. Calvin rejects the common rendering of the first verb as a summons to arms and argues instead for not wavering; he distinguishes two kinds of fear, one from the feeling of human nature even where faith is perfect, the other from faith’s weakness, so that the prohibition forbids not fear but discouragement. To be faint is to melt away. On the firebrands he presses the diminution: not torches, which might have seemed something great, but ends of them, and these not burning but only smoking. Wesley agrees they have more of show and terror than strength; Ellicott says the flame was nearly out.

All notice the contempt in naming the northern king only by his father. Gill observes there were two parties and not three, one king unnamed and the other styled as though the son of a private person; Ellicott compares how men spoke scornfully of Saul as the son of Kish, and Saul of David as the son of Jesse, and calls Pekah an upstart who reached the throne by rebellion and murder, which is Wesley’s point exactly. Adam Clarke works the text: the word now is dropped by two manuscripts and several versions, and the clause naming Syria is missing from one and altered in another. On the intended puppet, Ellicott makes the name Aramaic, good is God, and infers an officer in Rezin’s army; Calvin says who he was cannot easily be learned, probably an Israelite hostile to the house of David. Ellicott reads the breach as an assault on the line of fortresses, Jerusalem never actually besieged; Calvin thinks the allies counted not on a siege of so strong a city but on terror producing immediate surrender. Against all of it stands the bare word: Calvin notes that God does not mitigate the danger but holds out its full extent before promising, and that the counsel shall be reduced to nothing, as if it had never been.
8:
The plain sense is agreed. John Gill and John Wesley take the two namings as a fixing of limits: Damascus was the metropolis of Syria, where the king had his palace and kept his court, and Samaria the chief city of the ten tribes; therefore, Wesley draws out, Jerusalem shall not become part of Rezin’s dominion, and he shall keep within his own bounds. John Calvin puts the same thought as a speech: those two kings shall have such limits as they have now, they aspire to thy kingdom, but I have set bounds they shall not pass. Charles Ellicott hears an implied comparison, the two hostile cities and their kings set against Jerusalem and its supreme King.

The date is the crux, and the three attempts at it do not agree. Ellicott, reckoning the prophecy to a year some seven centuries before the Christian era, brings the sixty-five years down to the point at which inscriptions show that Assurbanipal, co-regent with his father Esarhaddon, carried off the last remnant of the people of Samaria and peopled it with an alien race, completing what earlier kings had begun. Adam Clarke reaches the same reign by a different road, counting from the beginning of the reign of Ahaz, when the prophecy was delivered, to the total depopulation of the kingdom by Esarhaddon, who removed the remains of the tribes his predecessors had left; he supports it by the Jewish tradition that Manasseh was carried to Babylon in the twenty-second year of his reign, when that king was in the neighbourhood, and argues that this last removal is what ended Israel as a people separate from all others, since from that time they never returned in a body but were confounded with the people of Judah. Calvin will not reckon from the delivery of this message at all, since that leaves only twenty years; he reckons instead from an earlier prophet’s prediction of the same captivity, which he takes to have been generally known and its arithmetic public—sixteen years of Jotham, as many of Ahaz, six of Hezekiah down to the deportation, and twenty-seven of Uzziah after that earlier prophecy was published. On his view the number is a confirmation of a reckoning already current, and the prophets faithfully assisted each other so that by their united labours they might serve God; it also sharply reproves a nation that, warned of the destruction of its country and its name, thought the word of God had grown old in so few years and opened its mouth to devour Judah.

Clarke also proposes to rearrange the six lines. Three of them open with the same words, and he supposes a copyist’s eye slipped from the first to the third, so that the distich which belongs in the middle was added at the end; as the text stands the destruction is denounced first and the grandeur set out after, which is preposterous, and the ruin of the northern kingdom coheres not with the greatness of its ally alone but with its own. He notes manuscripts reading twenty-five, and others sixty. Ellicott mentions that bolder critics go further and reject the whole clause as a later insertion. On the closing warning, Calvin insists the two verbs differ in form and so in force: it is not that unbelief proves you unbelievers, but that unless you rely on the promise you will not be established—God will stand though men disbelieve him, and salvation is bound up with his word. Wesley reads it against the policy in view, that seeking to Assyria for succour is the consuming. Keil and Delitzsch supply the king’s answer, or rather his silence: he was probably silent because he carried a secret that consoled him more, an invisible help and a remote prospect being not enough, and he let the enthusiast talk on and had his own thoughts.
10:
Matthew Henry takes the offer as evidence of divine faithfulness: God tells us nothing but what he is able and ready to prove, and considers our frame, that living in a world of sense we require sensible proofs, which he has favoured us with in sacramental signs and seals. That he is called the God of a bad king Henry explains by covenant—Ahaz was a child of Abraham and David—and John Gill says the same, that the Lord was his God as he was God of the nation. John Calvin generalises: when God sees that his promises do not satisfy us he makes additions suited to our weakness, so that we not only hear him speak but behold his hand displayed; miracles added to the word are seals. On the range allowed, Henry notes the choice may be taken in air, earth or water, for God’s power is the same in all, and compares the fleece Gideon asked; Calvin presses the two directions as a claim of dominion wider than this world, reaching the dead in their graves. Adam Clarke observes that several ancient versions read the first as going deep to the grave.

The refusal is judged hypocrisy by everyone. John Wesley says flatly that declining lest he question the word was deep hypocrisy. Henry finds the true reason in the Assyrian dependence: relying on their forces and their gods, the king would not be beholden to the God of Israel, and refused a confirming sign because he had resolved to persist in unbelief. Hence Henry’s maxim, that a secret disaffection to God is often disguised with the specious colours of respect, and that those resolved not to trust God pretend they will not tempt him. Charles Ellicott hears the accents of faith and, not perhaps without a sneer, an almost verbatim quotation of the legal formula—was the prophet going to forget his own teaching and become a tempter to that sin?—while beneath the show of humble trust lay self-will and utter unfaith, the alliance being already resolved on. Gill adds the practical shape of it: he was unwilling to be still and quiet and make no preparation for war.

Calvin turns the excuse into a doctrine of signs. Do we tempt God when we accept what he offers? Certainly not; it is indeed the highest virtue to ask nothing beyond his word, but if he chooses to add anything, to reject the addition as superfluous is no small insult, as though his dealings with us were of no advantage and he did not know what we chiefly need. He applies it to the two ordinances of the gospel, which the fanatics of his own day disregarded as childish elements—which they cannot do without rejecting the whole gospel, since we must not separate what the Lord has joined. He guards the other side too: Gideon asked a sign uncommanded, but not at his own suggestion, and the example must not be abused by men whose forwardness would ask innumerable signs without reason. He distinguishes the extraordinary signs, in which the miracle itself is seen, from those in daily use, which contain no miracle. Calvin also finds a wider purpose in the forbearance, that God had in view not the unbelieving king only but the weak in whom there was a seed of godliness. On the address to the whole royal house, Ellicott suspects its older members had encouraged the Assyrian project and perhaps suggested the answer; Keil and Delitzsch raise instead the question who is speaking, since the narrative makes it God and what follows is the prophet’s own, and conclude that the prophet was the organ of God even where he expressly distinguished himself from him, obliged to speak though his word should be a savour of death. Henry marks the one contrast that hurts: the king would not say my God, but the prophet will.
13:
On the reproof, John Calvin reads the ancestral title as itself the sting: to be reckoned descendants of David would have been an honour had they imitated his piety, and it aggravates the baseness that the grace of God was rejected by the very family from which the salvation of the world would proceed. He draws a rule of method from the sequence—begin with doctrine, add proofs when plain teaching does not serve, and only then employ vehemence, which is the last remedy—and he explains the contrast between wearying men and wearying God by the excuse the ungodly still make, that it is only men who speak to us, a way of disparaging what comes from God. The change of pronoun is noticed by everyone. Charles Ellicott marks it against the earlier the Lord thy God and concludes the king has involved himself in a sentence of rejection; Calvin says the prophet now claims the name as peculiar to himself, testifying that he came only when sent and said only what he was commanded, a boldness which all ministers should have rooted in their hearts and which false prophets counterfeit with empty talk. Ellicott also hears the first half of the question voicing a widespread hopeless discontent, men being weary too of a corrupt misgovernment; John Wesley notes the whole house is reproved because they were the king’s counsellors, and John Gill that it is the prophet who speaks.

The sign itself divides them. Ellicott renders it not a virgin but the young woman, or perhaps the bride, observing that the noun carries the definite article, that though commonly used of the unmarried it strictly denotes one arrived at marriageable age, and that bride in the older English and German sense best marks its relation to the two Hebrew words used distinctively for virgin and for wife; he adds only that the prophecy has been very differently interpreted. The others take it of the Messiah without hesitation. Gill calls it a sign in heaven and earth at once, the Lord from heaven taking flesh on earth, buried in the heart of the earth and raised and ascended. Calvin canvasses and dismisses the alternatives: Hezekiah cannot be meant, since he must have been full-grown when the city was besieged; the prophet’s own son cannot, since the title is far too illustrious to be applied to any man; and those who propose some child born at the time as an obscure picture produce no strong arguments and never say who the child was.

He is harder on his own side than on his opponents. Commentators, he says, have been too much at their ease, merely asserting that the birth from the Virgin Mary is promised here without meeting the objection that a birth five hundred years off has nothing to do with assuring the king of present deliverance. His answer is that the promise of a Redeemer is the foundation on which all special promises are built, so that whenever God helped his ancient people he reconciled them through Christ, all the promises being in him Yea and Amen; the deliverance of the city depended on that manifestation. Gill and Wesley give the same argument in its simpler form—the promised birth presupposed the preservation of the city, nation and tribe in which it was to occur, so the further off the birth the longer the safety. Wesley adds that the name is meant to describe a nature and office, God and man meeting in one person, rather than to report what he would commonly be called. Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar, noting that the verb of naming is third person and not second, so the words are not addressed to the mother. Adam Clarke reports many manuscripts reading the divine name for the title used here, and many writing the child’s name as two words.
15:
One small particle carries the whole entry. Adam Clarke argues at length that rendering it that he may know or till he know leaves the two verses incoherent, since the second is joined to the first as a reason, and it is no reason for a child eating curds and honey through his infancy that the land should be cleared of enemies before that infancy ends—the supposition implies that part of the time was spent under war and siege, when such food would not be attainable. Following a suggestion he credits to Harmer, he renders it when he shall know, so that the second verse gives a plain reason for the first: the country of the two kings would be desolated, and the land recover the plenty that attends peace. He supports the sense from other passages where the particle marks the moment a thing happens, and holds that these foods are delicacies in the East and so denote plenty. Charles Ellicott allows either till he know or when he shall know, but reverses the meaning: by a strange inversion of the familiar associations of the phrase, spoken probably with a touch of the irony of paradox, the words describe not plenty but scarcity, fields and vineyards left uncultivated and a people flying to caves and mountains reduced to the food of a nomadic tribe; the butter is the clotted milk that has always been a delicacy with Arabs.

John Calvin takes the clause for neither purpose but as proof of a true human nature. Since it was altogether incredible that one who was God should be so born, and revolting to ordinary judgment, the marks of human nature are given to keep us from thinking some apparition is presented; he will be reared as children commonly are. Calvin presses the consequence hard: the phrase fixes the term up to which he is reared after the manner of a child, and so he was for a time deprived of understanding and endured our weaknesses, which he grounds in the report that he grew in wisdom as well as in stature—had only growth in stature been meant, ignorance need not follow, but wisdom is named. John Gill and John Wesley keep to the plain reading that these were the common food of children in that country, Gill adding that the word means the cream of milk as well as butter, and that the phrase marks the place and time of the birth in a land of plenty and peace.

On the child of the second verse the readings part again. Gill takes it of the son the prophet had been told to bring, who must answer some end in the prophecy, though he allows any new-born child and so the Messiah; Wesley is certain it is that son, pointed at and brought by special command for this very use. Ellicott reads it of the age of approaching manhood, and insists the knowledge meant is moral choice rather than, as some critics hold, an infant’s discernment of food as pleasant or otherwise. Calvin says outright that he differs from all the commentators: the article marks the age and not a particular child, for had one been meant a demonstrative would have been added, and it would be absurd to defer a promised overturn of two kingdoms five hundred years. He also declines the causal rendering of the opening particle, taking the prophet to return here from a digression. On the outcome all agree and the histories are cited: Keil and Delitzsch note the two lands were wasted by the very power the king summoned, Calvin that one king fell then and the other died a few years later, Wesley that both lost their lands and their lives within two years. Ellicott finds the fulfilment the more remarkable for following what had seemed an almost decisive victory, which the prophet never mentions.
17:
Matthew Henry reads the turn as the second half of a single dealing: comfortable promises were made to the king as a branch of the house of David, and now terrible threatenings follow against him as a degenerate branch of it, the loving-kindness not utterly taken away but the iniquity chastened with the rod—so that those who will not mix faith with the promises of God may expect to hear the alarms of his threatenings. He notes the reach of it, prince, people and royal family alike, a judgment entailed on posterity and going along with the royal blood, and unprecedented since the day the northern tribes departed; the longer men continue in sin, the sorer the punishments. Charles Ellicott hears the prophet reading the secret thoughts of the heart and holding back the name of the king until the close of the sentence, with all the emphasis of suddenness, and observes that the old division is here used as a chronological era, the coming invasion being worse than any since. John Calvin presses the hypocrisy: the man who would not tempt God had called in those the Lord had forbidden him to call, and what he hopes will preserve him will destroy him. John Wesley divides the threat between the king, whose reign took part of the storm, and his successors; John Gill notes that the very power sent to for help distressed him instead.

Henry adds the terms of the bargain, that the king meanly promised to be a servant and made a present of gold and silver drained from the treasuries of both church and state—so the reed not only broke under him but ran into his hand and pierced it, and the creature we make our hope commonly proves our hurt. Calvin draws the harder lesson, that the covenant people themselves, who might have claimed exemption on the ground of privilege, are exposed to the same calamities, since God spares his Church and provides for her permanent existence without letting the wicked mingled among the good escape unpunished; the wonder is that amid such deaths the Church remains safe.

On the summons, Keil and Delitzsch match the figures to the nations: the one with its vast and unparalleled numbers to the swarming fly, the other with its love of war and conquest to the stinging bee. Calvin grounds the same metaphor in climate, one country hot and marshy and full of flies, the other abounding in bees, and takes the whistling to mean there will be no need of great exertion—at the sign they will instantly run. Wesley reads the plural rivers of the great river’s greatness or its several mouths, and the bees for numerous forces and orderly march as well as fierce attempts. Ellicott finds in the naming of the southern power a hint that some counsellors were already planning that alliance while others leaned on the northern one, the prophet telling them each is fraught with danger, since his one counsel from first to last is that men practise righteousness and wait upon the Lord. Adam Clarke simply lists the kings who one after another desolated the country, and prefers caverns for the holes.

Henry pictures the occupation: they find no difficulty forcing their way, resting in valleys the inhabitants had deserted at the first alarm, sheltering in the holes of rocks and showing themselves upon every thorn, so that the land is overspread. Wesley notes the valleys were fruitful before they were made desolate and the rocks perhaps a refuge. Ellicott makes the adjective mean steeply walled and the noun a torrent valley, the whole a graphic description of the country. Calvin declines to press the details, the language being figurative, and turns instead to providence: nothing happens at random, and God keeps a concealed bridle on furious beasts so they cannot break beyond the limits he prescribes.
20:
Adam Clarke calls the shaving highly parabolical, denoting the utter devastation of the country from one end to the other and the plundering of the people from the highest to the lowest, and he reads the three parts as ranks: the hairs of the head are those of the highest order in the state, the feet are the common people, the beard is the king and the high priest, the very supreme in dignity. He fills out the insult from custom and travel, for the beard has always been held in the highest veneration in the East and to pluck it is the greatest indignity that can be offered—he recalls the servants whose beards were half cut off and who were told to stay away until they were grown again, reports that men there swear by the beard, and cites a wounded man who hazarded his life rather than let a surgeon take it off. Charles Ellicott reads the article rather than an indefinite razor, refers the hiring to the tribute about to be paid, and turns it against the payer: he thought he was securing an ally, and was only hiring a razor—perhaps with the implied thought that the razor is in other hands than his—which would sweep away every sign of strength and leave him an open shame to all who looked on. He suspects an allusion to the shaving prescribed for a cleansed leper, the nation being leprous in its guilt.

John Calvin presses the word hired hardest. A man who uses a borrowed horse or sword uses it the more freely and does not spare it as he would his own, wishing the full value of what he pays for; so God threatens that he will not spare this instrument though he blunt it, sending its wielders with mad violence. Calvin also insists the great river will not hinder them, and that this is no portion of a nation wandering without a settled leader but the king himself at their head. John Gill takes the hire either of the present sent to buy help, or of the wages God later paid another conqueror, a thought Clarke states as a principle, that God considered the great nations he employed as his mercenaries and paid them their wages. John Wesley puts it as poetic justice, that they were scourged with a rod of their own making.

What follows divides the readers. Calvin reports three expositions of the milk: that one cow would scarcely feed a family, which makes it poverty; that however few the cattle there would be ample support, which makes it a promise; and his own, that the people will be so few that a little milk suffices them all, since it is a far heavier affliction for a country to want inhabitants than to want herds—and a promise here would be inappropriate. He adds that the man who keeps one cow and two sheep is not the poor man but the rich, reduced from large flocks to a remnant, which is Wesley’s point too, that those who kept great herds shall count it happiness to keep so few. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same as the most miserable housekeeping, the finest full-grown cattle having fallen to the foe, so that one cow and a couple of sheep are kept alive with the greatest care—yet enough, since all the land is now pasture. Bread and wine would be unattainable, and whoever escaped the razor would eat thickened milk and honey without variation to the point of nausea. Ellicott hears the irony in the word abundance and in the echo of the proverbial praise of the land. Gill declines to date the scene to the reign after this one, when plenty did follow a deliverance, and places it instead after the later fall of the city, when poor men were left to till the ground.
23:
The valuation is disputed before the desolation is. Charles Ellicott takes the thousand pieces as the rent of the vines at a shekel each, apparently a high rent and so indicating a choice quality of vine, and notes that the same figure elsewhere in scripture stands for the annual produce of a vineyard rather than its rent, a difference he thinks worth recording as bearing on the date of that other book; he adds that silverling was an old English word for any silver coin, used by the early translators, and that the going rate for a vine in his own day was a fraction of the old one. John Wesley reads it the other way, that each of the thousand vineyards might have been sold or let for a thousand shekels, which was the yearly rent of some excellent vineyards. John Calvin refuses the reading that makes a thousand vines worth a thousand pieces, since that would be far too low a price—who would reckon a shekel the value of a vineyard, the most precious of all possessions? It answers to the common phrase for selling at a trifle. Any field, however barren, would fetch more where the population is crowded; the collapse of the price is itself the reason he gives, for the inhabitants will be so few that you will scarcely find one to offer the smallest coin for the most valuable estates. John Gill puts the same cause plainly, that the ground goes barren for want of men to till it. Calvin also refuses, twice over and without argument, the reading that finds comfort for believers here.

The bows admit of several senses. Ellicott lists three—that the invaders march through the ruined vineyards shooting down whom they find, that the people carry bows for protection against the invaders, or that the thickets become coverts for beasts of prey and men need weapons against them—and judges the last has most in its favour. Gill reports the same range from earlier interpreters, fear of wild beasts and serpents, hunting them, or the danger from thieves; Wesley allows either hunting or defence, wild beasts commonly abiding in desolate grounds. Calvin, who reads the singular verb as a plural of archers marching through, sets aside the notion of husbandmen going armed because no unarmed man would dare approach his own land, and prefers the sharper irony that where the richest cultivation once stood there will now be good hunting, since the wild beasts have their dens there: the ground will be approached not by husbandmen but by hunters, who will not dress vines but chase game.

Ellicott reads the last verse as completing the picture—hillsides once brought under careful culture inch by inch will not be entered, since there is no use hoeing a tangled mass of brushwood, and they must be left to what pasturage cattle can find while their trampling increases the mischief. He notes that the received rendering instead makes the cultivated hills an exception to the general desolation, in which case a spiritual sense might be drawn from it. Wesley has the fences broken down and the owners slain or carried away, so that all sorts of cattle may enter. Calvin faces the apparent contradiction directly: having described desolation he now seems to describe a new condition, and some make it consolation, but his sense is that mountains formerly remote and hard of access become pasture because men crowd to them—a most wretched state, when men cannot escape death but by resorting to the wilderness. He ends on the king, who no doubt despised all this and settled on his lees once the siege lifted, and on the prophet’s duty to persevere and tell him that his destruction would come from the quarter whence he expected his preservation.
